This appendix offers practical guidance for migrating existing data workflows to Ibis,
including translation guides from pandas, SQL, and dplyr.

## Migrating from Other Tools

Here's how common data operations translate to Ibis using the World of Warcraft dataset:

```{python}
import ibis
from ibis import _

wowah = ibis.examples.wowah_data_raw.fetch()

# SQL to Ibis translation
# SQL: SELECT race, AVG(level) as avg_level FROM wowah
#      WHERE level > 10 GROUP BY race ORDER BY avg_level DESC;
sql_to_ibis = (
wowah
.filter(_.level > 10)
.group_by(_.race)
.aggregate(avg_level=_.level.mean())
.order_by(_.avg_level.desc())
)

# pandas to Ibis translation
# df[df['level'] > 10].groupby('race')['level'].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
pandas_to_ibis = (
wowah
.filter(_.level > 10)
.group_by(_.race)
.aggregate(avg_level=_.level.mean())
.order_by(_.avg_level.desc())
)

# dplyr (R) to Ibis translation
# wowah %>% filter(level > 10) %>% group_by(race) %>%
# summarize(avg_level = mean(level)) %>% arrange(desc(avg_level))
dplyr_to_ibis = (
wowah
.filter(_.level > 10)
.group_by(_.race)
.aggregate(avg_level=_.level.mean())
.order_by(_.avg_level.desc())
)

result = sql_to_ibis.execute()
print(result)
```

Key migration patterns: use `.filter()` instead of WHERE clauses, use
`.group_by().aggregate()` instead of GROUP BY, use `.order_by()` instead of ORDER BY,
and use method chaining instead of nested functions. The Ibis syntax is consistent
across all backends, making migration straightforward.
